item.title: How Databricks Autoscaling Actually Works (and Where It Leaves Compute Running)
item.description: Databricks autoscaling scales down after 40 or 150 seconds of underutilization. See what triggers scale-up, what the timer does, and how to resize by hand.
item.content:encoded:
You turned on Databricks autoscaling to stop paying for workers you aren't using. But when a job finishes, the cluster doesn't shrink right away. It keeps its workers for a set window first, which is 40 seconds on job compute and 150 seconds on all-purpose compute.

The setting that controls it, spark.databricks.aggressiveWindowDownS, is only documented for making that wait longer. If you want workers gone sooner, you resize the cluster yourself. Cutting idle compute is one of the five habits that move a Databricks bill, and autoscaling is one layer of the full cost optimization framework.

TL;DR

  • Databricks has three features called autoscaling, one for classic clusters, one for Lakeflow pipelines, and one for Lakebase. This article covers the first, which runs on job and all-purpose clusters.
  • A job cluster scales up on pending tasks against available task slots, so CPU graphs alone won't tell you when it will grow.
  • It scales down after 40 seconds of underutilization on job compute and 150 seconds on all-purpose compute.
  • The timer setting, spark.databricks.aggressiveWindowDownS, is documented only for slowing scale-down.
  • To change the worker count on a running cluster, use databricks clusters resize. databricks clusters edit restarts the cluster.

Which "Databricks autoscaling" are you even asking about?

Databricks uses the name autoscaling for three separate features, each on a different kind of compute. Before you tune anything, check which one you have.

The three kinds of Databricks autoscaling

  • Classic compute autoscaling runs on job and all-purpose clusters. It moves the worker count between a minimum and a maximum you set, based on pending tasks and available task slots.
  • Enhanced autoscaling runs on Lakeflow pipelines and scales on task slot utilization and task queue size.
  • Lakebase autoscaling resizes a Postgres compute inside a range of Compute Units (CU) that you set, based on CPU load, memory usage, and working set size. It also has a separate scale to zero feature that suspends an idle compute.

Three Databricks features share the name autoscaling. This article covers the first.

This article covers cluster autoscaling on classic compute. If you're sizing a Postgres database, read our Lakebase guide.

How does classic autoscaling decide to scale up?

A job cluster adds workers when Spark has more tasks pending than task slots to run them. Autoscaling decides from Spark scheduler signals, so CPU percentage alone won't tell you when a cluster is about to grow.

All-purpose clusters use the same autoscaler. On the Premium plan or above, every cluster type uses optimized autoscaling by default, and it can scale from minimum to maximum in at most two scaling events. Standard plan workspaces use standard autoscaling, which starts by adding eight nodes and then scales up exponentially.

Two limits apply before you rely on it. Autoscaling isn't available for spark-submit jobs. And a cluster can drop below your minimum when the cloud provider terminates instances, in which case Databricks keeps retrying until the minimum is restored.

Everything below describes optimized autoscaling on AWS and Azure.

Here's the baseline cluster spec, with an autoscaling range of 2 to 10 workers. Swap the two uppercase placeholders for a runtime version and a node type from your own workspace.

Worker count is only part of what a cluster costs. The rate each worker bills at counts too. On classic clusters, Photon-enabled compute consumes Databricks Units (DBUs) at a higher rate than equivalent non-Photon compute, and Photon's DBU math shows when that pays off.

Why does Databricks wait to let idle workers go?

Databricks waits because scale-down runs on a window. A job cluster will scale down once it has been underutilized for 40 seconds, and an all-purpose cluster after 150 seconds. So an all-purpose cluster that holds its size for a couple of minutes after a job ends is behaving normally.

A Spark configuration property, spark.databricks.aggressiveWindowDownS, sets in seconds how often the cluster makes down-scaling decisions. You set it in the cluster's Spark config, and the maximum is 600.

Scale-down doesn't need the whole cluster to go quiet. Optimized autoscaling can remove workers while the cluster is still busy by checking the shuffle file state, and how far it will scale down is based on a percentage of the current nodes. Streaming is different. Autoscaling has limits when scaling down Structured Streaming workloads, and Databricks recommends pipelines with enhanced autoscaling for those.

The window helps bursty workloads. A higher value holds onto nodes longer, through the short idle gaps between stages.

Raising the value makes the cluster scale down more slowly. Lower values are undocumented, so don't build a cost plan on one.

Here's the baseline spec with the property set to 300 seconds, for a bursty workload.

Does the default suit a team that answers for the bill? We think it does. A higher value keeps idle workers running longer, and you pay for them while they run. We'd only raise it for a bursty workload, to hold workers through the short gaps between stages.

Autoscaling is one setting among many. Download our free ebook, The Guide to Databricks Cost Optimization, for five core strategies and a decision tree that maps your specific cost problem to the right fix.

How do you resize a running cluster to release workers?

Use databricks clusters resize, the Databricks command-line interface (CLI) command for changing the worker count on a running cluster. Set the cluster to its minimum, then set the autoscale range again when work resumes.

The first command resizes the cluster to a fixed number of workers, and it only works while the cluster is running. The second sets the autoscale range again. It passes the cluster ID inside the JSON because the CLI doesn't accept a positional argument alongside --json.

It takes two commands because an autoscale range can't be a single number. In the Clusters API, max_workers must be strictly greater than min_workers, so you set a fixed count of 2 and set the range again later.

Don't use databricks clusters edit here. Editing a running cluster restarts it, and clusters created by the Jobs service can't be edited at all.

Try this on a non-production cluster first. The moments to use it are the ones where you know no work is coming, like the end of a batch window or the start of a maintenance freeze.

Skip it on all-purpose clusters that people query through the day. You can't predict the next request there, so the 150-second window is the better guard.

If dropping to the floor is safe at the end of every batch window, why is someone on your team still doing it by hand? We don't think they should be. A step that's safe every time, and only happens when someone remembers it, is a step to automate.

What happens when new work shows up?

When work returns, the cluster needs workers again, and new nodes take time to provision. After a resize from 5 to 10 workers, for example, the target size updates at once while the workers increase gradually as nodes come up.

An instance pool shortens that wait by keeping idle instances ready, but only if the pool is big enough. If the cluster asks for more than the pool's minimum number of idle instances, it starts no faster than a cluster without a pool.

Idle pool instances still add to your costs. Setting Min Idle instances to 0 avoids paying for instances that aren't doing work, and the Idle Instance Auto Termination time controls how long a released instance stays in the pool before it's dropped.

Which anti-pattern breaks all of this?

The anti-pattern is enabling Apache Spark Dynamic Allocation (spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled) on a cluster that already uses Databricks autoscaling.

Databricks autoscaling already manages worker nodes and executor lifecycle at the platform level, so turning on Dynamic Allocation gives you two systems making the same call. That can cause conflicting scaling decisions, executor churn, NODES_LOST errors, and tasks that are never picked up.

If you see either symptom on an autoscaling cluster, check for that setting first. Remove it from the cluster's Spark config, and check your compute policies too, since workspace admins can use them to enforce Spark configurations.

Autoscaling changes the worker count. Shutting down an idle cluster is a different job, and auto termination is a separate control.

What does doing this by hand cost, and what does SELECT automate?

Everything above is engineering time. You read a cluster spec, set a Spark config, run a resize at the end of the batch window, and run another one when work resumes. Then you do it again for the next cluster. And autoscaling parameters are only one of the cluster choices that shape your bill, next to cluster size, instance type, and spot instance usage. We count autoscaling in the easy wins tier of Databricks cost work.

That's the work we built Automated Savings to take over. SELECT's Automated Savings for Databricks automatically adjusts worker count and auto-scaling behavior to reduce costs on SQL warehouses and All-Purpose Compute. We report savings of up to 30 percent on eligible workloads, with no ongoing engineering effort. The Optimize chapter of our ebook goes deeper on this layer.

Is running these steps by hand a defensible trade, or a cost that compounds as your clusters and schedules multiply? That call is yours. Our view: for one or two clusters on a fixed schedule, doing it by hand is a fair trade. Past that, every new cluster adds another resize someone has to remember, and that's the cost that compounds.

To see your own savings potential, book a demo or start a free trial.

item.title: Databricks Cost Optimization Tools Compared
item.description: Compare Databricks cost optimization tools by write access, scope, and pricing, from Governance Hub and LakeSentry to Sedai, Unravel, Flexera, and SELECT.
item.content:encoded:
If you lead platform or data engineering and are weighing Databricks cost optimization tools, start by asking what a paid tool adds beyond Databricks. Databricks' announcement of Governance Hub describes FinOps (Financial Operations) leads drilling into spend and identifying its drivers without maintaining dozens of queries and dashboards. Governance Hub brings that analysis into the account console.

The right tool for you depends on your estate and how much control you want it to have over your Databricks resources. This guide compares four categories based on write access, scope, and public pricing. Write access shows you what the tool can change, while scope indicates whether it works only with Databricks or across several platforms. Each tool is classified by the write-access model its vendor describes.

TL;DR

  • Native controls and Governance Hub (Beta) show your total Databricks spend and how much of it is tagged.
  • Cost intelligence platforms such as LakeSentry give you job- and team-level attribution, anomaly detection, and prioritized actions for your team to apply.
  • Autonomous engines such as Sedai, Altimate, Capital One Slingshot, Unravel, and SELECT can modify your Databricks resources for you, with approval levels that vary by tool.
  • Broad FinOps platforms such as Flexera combine your Databricks costs with cloud and data platform spend.
  • Choosing between them comes down to how much authority you give a tool to modify your Databricks resources.

Do you still need Databricks cost optimization tools in 2026?

You still need a paid tool if Governance Hub leaves work undone for your team. Governance Hub entered Beta in July 2026 and was announced publicly in August.

Governance Hub changes how you evaluate paid tools. Its Cost page shows you where your money goes. If you need attribution down to the user or query, or want optimizations applied to your resources for you, you need more than the Cost page offers.

To determine what you need, start with the five habits in Databricks cost optimization actually explained, which outline the work involved in reducing Databricks costs. The FinOps Foundation's Inform, Optimize, and Operate phases show where that work sits, with Inform examining cost and usage data, Optimize identifying efficiency opportunities, and Operate implementing the changes. Whatever Governance Hub does not cover across those habits and phases is what a paid tool has to add.

What are the four categories of Databricks cost tooling?

Databricks cost optimization tools fall into four categories: native controls, cost intelligence platforms, autonomous optimization engines, and broad FinOps platforms. Each is sorted by what the tool is allowed to change and how many platforms it covers. LakeSentry's comparison page uses a near-identical four-group split, so this framework is not unique to this guide, and it is not an industry standard.

Native controls are the cost tools included with Databricks. System tables and Governance Hub Cost read your usage data and cannot change your compute, while budgets and compute policies are the limits you set yourself.

Cost intelligence platforms build on that data with attribution, anomaly detection, and prioritized actions. LakeSentry is a Databricks-only example, and it is read-only by default, so your team decides whether to act.

Autonomous optimization engines can make resource changes. Sedai, Altimate, Capital One Slingshot, Unravel, and SELECT can resize warehouses or adjust clusters, with controls ranging from approval gates to automatic execution.

Broad FinOps platforms combine Databricks with AWS (Amazon Web Services), Azure, GCP (Google Cloud Platform), Snowflake, and other platform spend. Flexera is one example, and Databricks is one line among many in that view.

The categories differ mainly in write access and scope. The table below summarizes those differences alongside their pricing models.

CategoryWrite AccessScopePricing Model
Native controlsNo compute changes (budgets can be set)Databricks-onlyBuilt into Databricks
Cost intelligenceRead-only by defaultDatabricks-onlyPublic, listed
Autonomous optimization enginesApproval-gated to auto-applyMulti-platformVaries by vendor
Broad FinOpsRecommendations onlyMulti-platformNot published on the product page

What do System Tables and the new Governance Hub cover?

Native controls give you detailed visibility into Databricks spend. System tables provide the underlying billing data, while Governance Hub adds an account-level view on top.

In the billing system tables, system.billing.usage records billable usage, including the Databricks Units (DBUs) consumed, and joining it with system.billing.list_prices converts that usage into list-price dollars. You attribute that spend to a team or project with tags, which compute policies enforce on classic compute and serverless usage policies apply on serverless compute.

Governance Hub includes Data, AI (artificial intelligence), Cost, and Tags pages, and Cost is the one that applies here. It adds a spend explorer for viewing costs by product, workspace, resource, or tag, along with tagged-spend tracking and budgets that workspace admins create and manage for their workspaces. Its cost recommendations are read-only, and every amount on the Cost page is shown at list price, so your negotiated discounts do not appear.

In Governance Hub, you can ask Genie questions such as why costs spiked and get answers grounded in your governance data. Databricks' August 2026 announcement says Genie will soon take actions such as configuring policies, setting up alerts, and implementing recommendations. As of that announcement, Genie explains and does not act.

system.billing.usage covers Databricks charges only, while classic compute also incurs cloud-provider charges for the underlying virtual machines. If you run classic compute, you need both Databricks billing data and cloud-provider costs to calculate the full compute cost. Databricks' February 2026 blog post on unifying Databricks and cloud infrastructure costs introduces an open source solution that joins the two on AWS and Azure.

What does LakeSentry add in the Databricks-only cost intelligence category?

LakeSentry adds job- and team-level attribution, anomaly detection, and prioritized actions on top of your system table data. It connects through a read-only service principal, and its GetApp listing says it attributes spend across workspaces and environments by job and team.

For cost spikes, LakeSentry compares recent spend against a baseline using z-scores, with minimum cost thresholds so small workloads do not raise findings, as its anomaly detection docs describe. Each finding shows its evidence, such as the baseline and the cost increase.

Pricing is public and based on user count. Free supports one user, Standard costs $499 per month for up to five users, and Pro costs $849 per month for unlimited users, with paid plans billed annually. All plans include unlimited workspaces, and pricing does not depend on DBU usage or workspace count. The pricing page also lists "Safe optimization" on every plan, so ask the vendor what that includes and which write-access model applies before you connect.

LakeSentry also publishes a comparison of Databricks cost tools, last updated August 5, 2026. It places LakeSentry in a cost-intelligence category and groups Unravel with broader efficiency and FinOps platforms. This guide places Unravel with autonomous engines because its Arvix AI engine can apply changes, while LakeSentry's own table describes Unravel as using autonomous remediation.

Because LakeSentry sells one of the products being compared, treat that categorization as the vendor's view and check it against independent sources.

How do Sedai, Altimate, Slingshot, and Unravel handle autonomous optimization?

Sedai, Altimate, Slingshot, and Unravel each let you hand Databricks optimization changes to software, but they differ in how much control you keep, from automatic execution to approval gates and per-job settings.

Sedai

Sedai says you can connect your cloud and monitoring accounts in under 15 minutes. In copilot mode you approve each change with one click, or you can let optimizations run automatically. Sedai's June 2025 launch announcement places Databricks alongside AWS, Azure, GCP, and Kubernetes and cites cloud cost reductions of 30% or more across its platform. Its Databricks page advertises 30 to 50%.

Altimate

Altimate's Auto Tune agents use approval gates, with controls available per job, task, and warehouse, according to Altimate's guide. Altimate's Databricks page reports a typical reduction of 20 to 35%, and Auto Tune rolls back changes that degrade performance automatically.

Capital One Slingshot

Slingshot gives you job-level control through technology from Sync Computing, whose team joined Capital One Software in 2025. According to Capital One's Databricks announcement, you can apply an optimization in one click or fully automate it, and Slingshot's documentation shows that each job's project has its own auto-apply setting, so different jobs in the same deployment can run at different levels of automation.

Unravel

Unravel covers Databricks, Snowflake, and BigQuery. Its Arvix AI engine can rewrite code, rightsize compute, and clean up storage. It tests each change against workload behavior before applying it and reverts automatically if performance declines.

What to check before you automate changes

Vendors give you different levels of control over automated changes, from manual approvals to automatic execution. Before you connect a tool, confirm when a change requires your approval, when it can act automatically, and what happens if a change causes problems.

For any tool you consider, including SELECT, check which permissions it holds, which resources it can change, its rollback capabilities, and the audit trail it provides. Also check how those changes enter your deployment process, because settings changed outside infrastructure as code can drift from the configuration you defined. SELECT's setup guide requires CAN_MANAGE on jobs, clusters, and warehouses when Automated Savings is enabled.

Where does Flexera fit in broad multi-cloud FinOps?

Flexera fits when you want your Databricks costs in the same view as the rest of your cloud and data platform spend, and its Databricks product recommends changes instead of making them. The autonomous engines above are built to change resources, while Flexera focuses on FinOps across multiple cloud and data platforms and gives you one consolidated view of your costs.

Flexera One Data Cloud Optimization is the product formerly known as Chaos Genius, which Flexera acquired in January 2026. It provides Databricks and Snowflake rightsizing guidance within a FinOps suite for budgeting and forecasting. Flexera's June 2026 release notes describe a Databricks Analyzer dashboard that combines DBU spend with the underlying cloud infrastructure compute cost, giving you a unified view of platform and compute spend.

Flexera's acquisition announcement says Chaos Genius has helped Fortune 500 enterprises reduce costs by up to 30% and describes the product as autonomous, agentic optimization. Its Data Cloud Optimization documentation focuses on visibility, allocation, and savings recommendations, so this guide treats its documented Databricks workflow as recommendation-led unless Flexera documents specific write actions. Flexera does not publish pricing on its product page.

Where does SELECT fit, and what are its limits?

SELECT fits when you want continuous, toggle-controlled changes to Databricks worker counts and autoscaling. It does not report your cloud infrastructure bill or rewrite your code. The key questions are what it can see, what it can change, and where its limits are.

SELECT breaks down Databricks spend by workspace, workload type, job, cluster, user, and query, according to its Databricks launch changelog. Once you configure it, Automated Savings adjusts worker counts and autoscaling for All-Purpose Compute and SQL Warehouses without day-to-day tuning. This guide places SELECT in the autonomous category because that write access is continuous and toggle-controlled. SELECT reports savings of up to 30% on eligible workloads.

SELECT reports Databricks platform spend using Databricks billing and list-price system tables, so you account for cloud infrastructure costs separately. SELECT's guide to Databricks cost optimization gives you a rule of thumb for estimating those costs alongside your DBU bill.

Treat Governance Hub as your baseline. Its Cost page shows amounts at list price, while SELECT's custom rates let you include negotiated discounts in your numbers. SELECT also attributes spend down to the user and query, and Automated Savings acts where Governance Hub's read-only recommendations stop.

Know the limits before you buy. SELECT does not rewrite code, and Unravel's May 2026 launch material says Arvix AI does. Pricing starts at $1,499 per month, and the final quote depends on your environment, so Governance Hub may be enough for a smaller estate.

Which category fits your team?

Choose based on how much authority you are willing to give a tool to modify your Databricks resources. If you mainly need better visibility, start with native controls and Governance Hub, which leave changes in your hands. Governance Hub is in Beta as of October 2026. If you also need attribution and anomaly detection while keeping changes in-house, add a cost intelligence platform such as LakeSentry.

If you want changes applied for you, choose an autonomous engine. Control varies by tool, from approval gates to automatic execution and rollback, so decide how much automation each workload should get. If you run Databricks alongside other platforms, choose a broad FinOps platform such as Flexera, which puts Databricks alongside the rest of your cloud and data platform spend.

Before you pay for another tool, check what Governance Hub already provides and what the additional tool adds. SELECT's post on what to do beyond the easy wins covers the next layer once the basics are in place. If you want to evaluate SELECT in your environment, you can connect a workspace, which SELECT says takes about 20 minutes, or book a demo.

item.title: Serverless SQL Warehouse Cost Optimization
item.description: Learn which SQL Warehouse setting to change first: auto-stop, size, max clusters, or Power BI mode, and how Serverless, Pro, and Classic compare.
item.content:encoded:
You can reduce Databricks Serverless SQL Warehouse cost by matching each workload problem to the right control. Auto-stop reduces inactive runtime, warehouse size affects single-query performance, and max clusters controls how much concurrency the warehouse can absorb.

The challenge is that those signals often get mixed together. A warehouse that stays active between short jobs does not need more horsepower. Workloads waiting for capacity may need more clusters rather than a larger warehouse. Power BI DirectQuery can also keep generating Databricks SQL activity even when the SQL itself is already well optimized.

This article shows you how to tell those cases apart, compare Serverless with Pro and Classic using total cost rather than DBU price alone, and choose the setting that matches the behavior you are actually seeing. These warehouse-level decisions sit inside the full Databricks cost optimization framework, where sizing, utilization, attribution, and automation work together.

TL;DR

  • Auto-stop reduces idle windows between bursts of SQL work.
  • Warehouse size controls the compute available to individual queries.
  • Max clusters controls how much concurrent demand the warehouse can serve.
  • Serverless, Pro, and Classic need to be compared on total workload cost, not DBU price alone.
  • Power BI connection mode can materially change SQL Warehouse activity when DirectQuery is used for freshness the business does not need.

Why startups and idle time drive Databricks SQL Warehouse cost

Your SQL Warehouse bill can grow faster than query runtime suggests because short jobs still create startups and active windows. Scheduled alerts make the problem easy to miss: several sub-minute queries on separate schedules can keep a Databricks Serverless SQL Warehouse active far longer than the SQL itself runs. Configuration can make that gap worse. One documented bundle deployment omitted auto_stop_mins and ended up with a 120-minute value, even though current Databricks Declarative Automation Bundles documentation lists a 10-minute Serverless default.

Our read is that a hidden configuration mistake can do more damage than one slow query because it repeats across every run. How much of your SQL Warehouse bill comes from expensive queries, and how much comes from settings nobody has revisited? The same pattern appears in the five habits that move a Databricks bill and the full cost optimization framework.

Databricks SQL warehouse types: Serverless vs. Pro vs. Classic

Across the main SQL warehouse types, Serverless has the highest visible Databricks Unit (DBU) rate because its price includes the underlying infrastructure. A Pro SQL warehouse has a lower DBU rate, and Classic the lowest, but both charge for cloud infrastructure separately. With serverless compute, Databricks manages the underlying infrastructure rather than exposing a separate cloud infrastructure charge for you to manage.

For example, published AWS Premium list rates in US East put Serverless at about $0.70 per DBU, a Pro SQL warehouse at $0.55, and Classic at $0.22 as of 2026. Actual rates can vary by cloud, region, edition, and contract. Those figures apply to one regional pricing example, but they show why the DBU rate alone does not tell you which option costs less overall.

TypeRelative DBU rateInfrastructure billingCold startBest fit
ServerlessHighestIncludedTypically secondsBursty, interactive BI and DirectQuery workloads
ProMid-rangeBilled separatelyTypically minutesPredictable BI workloads that need Pro features
ClassicLowestBilled separatelyTypically minutesPredictable scheduled workloads

Serverless SQL warehouses are better suited to bursty demand because they can start within seconds and respond quickly as demand changes. Databricks SQL Serverless also uses Intelligent Workload Management (IWM) to predict query resource needs and manage capacity as demand changes. That reduces the need to keep compute warm just to avoid a long startup delay.

Pro SQL warehouses and Classic SQL warehouses are more relevant when demand is predictable. Databricks recommends these SQL warehouses for scheduled Import or Extract jobs where demand is easier to plan and rapid startup matters less. A Pro SQL warehouse adds capabilities beyond Classic SQL, which remains the lower-DBU option for simpler use cases.

The useful comparison is the total cost of running the workload, including infrastructure, startup behavior, and how long the warehouse needs to stay active. Looking only at the DBU rate creates the same half-bill mistake and can make Serverless look more expensive than it really is.

If you want to compare those costs at the warehouse level, SELECT for Databricks can help you see where SQL Warehouse spend, sizing, and utilization are coming from before you change the configuration.

SQL warehouse auto-stop: The UI and API floors differ

Serverless SQL warehouses give you more room to shorten auto-stop than Pro or Classic SQL warehouses. In the Databricks UI, the minimum for Serverless is five minutes, while the API and Declarative Automation Bundles can take auto_stop_mins down to one minute. Pro and Classic have a 10-minute minimum.

The shortest setting is not always the right one. A one-minute auto-stop can suit isolated scheduled jobs, while interactive DirectQuery workloads may benefit from staying warm longer. Our SQL Warehouse auto-stop guidance recommends roughly 10 minutes for general SQL use.

You can set a Serverless warehouse to a one-minute auto-stop with the Databricks CLI:

Defaults also depend on how you create SQL warehouses. The Databricks UI defaults Serverless to 10 minutes and Pro or Classic to 45 minutes, while Declarative Automation Bundles use 10 minutes for Serverless and 120 minutes for Pro or Classic. Set auto_stop_mins explicitly so the deployment does not depend on the default for that configuration path.

Sizing a SQL warehouse: Size vs. Clusters

In Databricks SQL, warehouse size and max clusters solve different performance problems. Size controls the compute available to individual queries, while max clusters controls how much concurrent demand the warehouse can serve. Serverless also uses Intelligent Workload Management to handle part of the resource allocation automatically.

Use query and queue signals to decide which control to adjust:

SymptomDial to turn
A single query is slow or spills heavily to diskIncrease warehouse size
Queries spend significant time waiting at capacityIncrease max clusters
Peak Queued Queries stays above zeroCheck both warehouse size and max clusters
Long inactive gaps between queriesLower auto-stop

Peak Queued Queries does not identify the exact fix on its own. High waiting_at_capacity_duration_ms points to capacity pressure, while slow or heavily spilling queries point more toward warehouse size. Our preference is to confirm whether the pressure is query-level or concurrency-level before adding more compute.

Idle time points to a different problem. When capacity is sufficient during query execution but the warehouse stays active between jobs, auto-stop is the setting to inspect.

When Power BI DirectQuery changes the serverless cost equation

Power BI DirectQuery can generate far more warehouse activity than the dashboard itself seems to justify because every interaction can send another query to Databricks. Databricks recommends Serverless SQL Warehouses for DirectQuery and LiveQuery, with a 15 to 30-minute auto-stop window for interactive workloads.

When the business only needs updates every few minutes, Import or Hybrid models can reduce Databricks SQL activity by serving more report interactions from Power BI itself. Materialized views can also precompute repeated SQL work, although their refreshes still use separate serverless compute.

Our view is that DirectQuery should be one of the first places you investigate when Serverless cost feels disconnected from dashboard complexity. Before blaming Serverless pricing, check whether the BI connection mode is creating more activity than the freshness requirement actually needs.

Turning these dials into a setting

Keeping SQL Warehouse cost under control requires ongoing visibility into sizing, idle time, and capacity pressure. Our SQL Warehouse cost view brings those signals together so you can see where configuration deserves another look.

Our Automated Savings can adjust supported worker-count and autoscaling settings for SQL Warehouses as demand changes. Auto-stop remains a separate control, so you should still review auto_stop_mins after deployments and audit BI connection modes when activity no longer matches the business freshness requirement.

The next tier of savings is turning those checks into an operating habit. The decision is whether reviewing size, max clusters, auto-stop, and BI modes by hand is still a defensible trade-off, or whether that recurring work is starting to compound.

Databricks Serverless SQL Warehouse cost: What to adjust first

Match the setting to the signal you are seeing: idle windows point to auto-stop, queue pressure to capacity, slow individual queries to warehouse size, and unexpected BI activity to the connection mode. Compare Serverless, Pro, and Classic on total cost rather than DBU price alone.

Review the evidence before changing configuration. Our Databricks cost view brings SQL Warehouse cost, sizing, idle compute, and utilization together so you can see which setting deserves attention first.

item.title: Best Practices for Hosting Streamlit Dashboards in Snowflake
item.description: Learn how Streamlit in Snowflake is billed, why container runtime wins, how to suspend nightly to cut credits, and when it beats Power BI.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

  • Container runtime is my default for hosting Streamlit in Snowflake. Dashboards stay warm, offering the best user experience.
  • A container runtime node costs 0.11 credits per hour, compared to 1 credit per hour for an XS warehouse. At $3 per credit, that is about $238 a month if always on. One node hosts three dashboards. The fourth one starts a new node.
  • To save even more, suspend the compute pool with a nightly task. The trade-off is that the first viewer of each dashboard or app each morning waits about 45 seconds.
  • After a suspend, only the dashboards people actually open resume billing. You pay for what gets used, not what is deployed.
  • For the price of 100 Power BI Premium Per User seats ($2,400 a month), Snowflake can host about 81 actively viewed Streamlit apps with the nightly suspend.

Intro

Streamlit is an open source Python library for creating data centric web apps or dashboards. You write Python, and you get charts, filters, buttons, modals, and interactivity without touching HTML or JavaScript. The Python-only approach to web apps has made Streamlit a very popular tool for data teams to ship internal tools.

Snowflake bought Streamlit in 2022, and Streamlit in Snowflake is the result. Your app runs inside your Snowflake account, right next to your data. There is no server to host, no separate login system, and no copying data out to somewhere else. Access follows the same roles you already manage.

There are now two ways to run a Streamlit app in Snowflake, and they charge you in very different ways. Pick the wrong one, or leave the right one running all night, and you pay for it.

This post covers how each option is billed, an auto-suspend gotcha that cost me real credits, how to suspend nightly, what that does to your bill (more than you would guess), and where the break-even sits against Power BI.

Two ways to run Streamlit in Snowflake

Warehouse runtime

The app runs on a virtual warehouse. You are billed for the time that warehouse is active. Each time a viewer connects, a new Streamlit server process starts in it, and a websocket keeps the warehouse awake until about 15 minutes after the viewer's last activity. The timeout is configurable so you can easily set it to time out after 5 minutes of inactivity. An XS warehouse burns 1 credit per hour while awake. Your SQL could run on a separate query warehouse, so you may have two warehouses consuming credits.

Container runtime

The app runs on a node in a compute pool that Snowflake manages for you. The Streamlit server runs continuously on that node, so pages load fast and every viewer shares the same server. This is truly the best user experience, as few users ever hit cold starts.

Snowflake supports both, and it is making container runtime the default for new apps.

My take: Using a warehouse runtime with a strict 5 minute timeout to save money is a poor user experience, as almost every visitor is getting a cold start. I’m using container runtime for all of my Streamlit apps so the dashboards are pre-warmed and cached after the first user views the page.

Same Streamlit code. Very different bill.

Choose the smallest compute possible to run the Streamlit process

Whether you choose the Warehouse runtime or the new default Container runtime, the Streamlit process itself does not need much horsepower. An Extra Small Gen 1 warehouse is enough to run any Streamlit app I’ve come across. The queries themselves can use a bigger warehouse, but don’t waste credits on the Streamlit process.

If you can develop the dashboard on your laptop, you can host it on an Extra Small or the default compute pool which runs CPU_X64_S.

How container runtime is billed

One node is one billing unit. On the default system CPU pool, Snowflake packs three dashboards onto one node. When a fourth dashboard is running, it spins up a second node. A seventh spins up a third. The pool grows in steps of three. (See Cost Scenarios section below for more examples.)

The smallest node costs about 0.11 credits per hour. That works out to:

  • 2.64 credits per day
  • about 79 credits per month
  • $7.92 per day or $237.6 per month at $3 per credit, if auto-suspend never kicks in.

Your credit price will differ, so swap in your own. I use $3 for every example below.

A few things to notice:

  • It is the same price for 1 viewer or 100 viewers. The node does not care. (Comparison to PowerBI Per User license pricing below!). This is a refreshing pricing model; I’m so tired of cost per user BI licensing.
  • A node is about 9x cheaper per hour than an XS warehouse. The catch is that the node stays on, and the warehouse does not. If one code warehouse would be awake more than about 2.6 hours a day, the node wins. If your dashboard gets opened twice a week, the warehouse wins.
  • A dashboard nobody has opened costs nothing. The app's service starts on its first view. Deploying 25 dashboards does not rent 9 nodes. Only the ones that get opened do.
  • Container runtime does not remove your query costs. The SQL still runs on a warehouse. This post only covers the cost of hosting the app.

I’ve had a great experience using Container Runtime for Streamlit with Adaptive Warehouses for the query execution. Per Snowflakes docs, Adaptive Warehouses are faster than Gen 2 warehouses.

How many nodes is my Streamlit Compute Pool running?

Streamlit apps are deployed to the default compute pool, system_compute_pool_cpu. You can check how many nodes are running in the UI, under Compute in the sidebar, then compute pools.

If you click into that row, it brings you to a details page where you can see what apps are running:

Then check the active_nodes column.

The auto-suspend gotcha

Here is what the docs say. After three days of viewer inactivity, the Streamlit server process ends. Then the compute pool suspends according to its own AUTO_SUSPEND value.

Two problems with that.

First, the three days is not configurable, yet. You cannot make it one day or one hour. Three days of an idle node is about 8 credits, or $24. Not a disaster on its own. But it adds up across a pool, and across every environment you deploy to.

Second, the pool's own AUTO_SUSPEND only starts counting when no services are running on it. The Streamlit service sits there until the three days are up, so the pool timer never gets a chance to help you.

As of October 15, 2026, auto-suspend does not reliably fire: I watched a service and its container run past day 3 and still be spending money on day 4, and Snowflake support told me the cause is browser tabs left open that keep retrying the websocket (even rejected 401 reconnects reset the idle timer on the backend). Snowflake is working on a fix, so by the time you read this it may already be solved.

There is a private preview feature that adds idle_auto_shutdown_time_seconds at the app level, like the warehouse runtime has. You may have seen the property show up when you describe a Streamlit app. Once you are enrolled, you can set it to a shorter value. Ask your Snowflake account team. I would love to be able to set this to a few hours for each app and have the leanest setup possible!

Until then, do not count on the three day timer. Suspend it yourself if you want to save. Let’s discuss this more.

Suspend nightly and let users wake it up

The simplest cost saving is a scheduled task that suspends the pool every evening:

The role that owns the task needs OPERATE on the pool. If you run it as a serverless task, it also needs EXECUTE MANAGED TASK.

In the morning, nobody has to do anything. The first person to open a dashboard wakes it up. In my experience that first load is about a 45 second cold start. After that, it is fast for everyone else.

The part people miss and where savings stack up

When you suspend the pool at night, every dashboard gets shut down. In the morning, only the ones people open come back, and only those start billing again.

Say you have 25 dashboards. If you leave everything running, you pay for 9 nodes, because over time someone opens every one of them. If you suspend at night and people only open 4 dashboards the next day, you pay for 2 nodes. The other 21 dashboards cost nothing that day.

That makes the nightly suspend a much more powerful trick than just saving the nightly hours you suspended for. You also stop paying for the dashboards nobody looks at. Month end reports, the quarterly review, the stale dashboard someone built for a project months ago: they only cost money on the days someone actually views them.

Your bill now follows how many dashboards get opened per day, not how many you have deployed.

Pros

  • Predictable bill. You know the worst case.
  • It works even while the auto-suspend bug exists.
  • One statement suspends every node in the pool, whether you have 3 dashboards or 30.
  • Rarely used dashboards stop costing money.
  • Nothing to remember. No one has to log in and stop things.

Cons

  • The first viewer of each dashboard each day waits about 45 seconds. My users are fine with this.
  • Anyone working late or on a weekend hits the same cold start.
  • Suspending drops every node on the pool. Anyone mid-session will suddenly hit a reboot page, so pick a time when people have gone home. In my opinion the risk is low and the refresh is quick enough to make it worth it.

If 45 seconds is too long for the people who open the dashboards first thing in the morning, you can send an authenticated request to those apps' endpoints a few minutes before they arrive. It worked for me, but it needs OAuth set up, which adds complexity. Warm only the few that matter, or you give back the savings on dashboards no one reads. To me, pre-warming the dashboards is more complicated than it is worth (due to needing OAuth flow), but the option is there.

Cost scenarios

Assumptions: $3 per credit, 25 dashboards deployed, three dashboards per node. "Suspended" means the nodes run 12 hours a day on weekdays only (22 days a month). That is an upper bound, because a dashboard opened at 2pm does not bill for the morning.

Now compare that to leaving all 25 running around the clock. Over time every dashboard gets opened, so you pay for 9 nodes, all month: $2,138. If only 4 dashboards get used on a typical day, the nightly suspend takes you from $2,138 to $174.

Pack your nodes. Dashboard number 4 costs you the same as dashboard number 6, so if you are going to pay for a second node, fill it.

Break-even vs Power BI

Power BI Pro is billed per user. At the $14 per user per month list price, every person who views a report needs a seat. Streamlit in Snowflake is billed per node. There is no platform fee and no seat fee.

So start from your headcount. Here is what Power BI costs at $24 per user per month (Premium), and how many dashboards the same money runs in Snowflake with the nightly suspend:

Read it like this. If 4 dashboards get used by 50 people, Power BI Pro is about $700 a month and Snowflake is $174. If 25 dashboards all get used by 40 people, Power BI is about $560 and Snowflake is $784, or $2,138 if you never suspend. The more people per dashboard, the better Snowflake looks. The more dashboards per person, the better Power BI looks.

Two honest caveats:

  • Streamlit is code. Power BI is drag and drop. If your analysts cannot write Python (or are not fully AI enabled), the hosting savings may not matter.
  • Power BI Premium Per User is $24 per user per month, and Fabric capacity removes the viewer seat for large deployments, but it starts around $5,000 a month. Check current prices before you build the business case.

Takeaways

  1. Use container runtime for dashboards people open frequently. Container runtime is my new default, as I prefer the cheaper per hour cost and I don’t want to comingle it with my Warehouse usage. I also like the user experience of fewer cold starts compared to Warehouses which you aggressively auto-suspend.
  2. Three dashboards per node. The fourth one starts a new node.
  3. The smallest node is about 0.11 credits per hour, 2.64 per day, about $238 a month at $3 per credit. Yes, the smallest node can host your dashboards, no problem. Data size does not matter; queries still run on Virtual Warehouses.
  4. Do not rely on the three day auto-suspend. Suspend the pool on a schedule.
  5. After a suspend, only the dashboards people open start billing again. You pay for what gets used, not what is deployed.
  6. Budget for a 45 second cold start, and tell your users about it.
  7. Past a few dozen viewers, per node billing beats per seat billing.
